A run made only of in-transit nights is not a trip. Without a place of kind home there are no trips, and the command says why. ADR 0019: a trip is never a line, only a reader's output, until the captain names it, and the name is a note/v1.
  • logbook rollup places|people: the two rollups that read company through the with module. places: per named place and per asset (the owner's stays aboard it), per year — stays, hours, first and last visit (the stay's start and end day), an asset's nights aboard, and the people confirmed present with their days and lines. people: per resolved person, per year — days together (days with confirmed evidence, by the evidence's own day), the last real contact (the last such day), the places shared (a named place, aboard <asset>, else coordinates), confirmed and proposed evidence counts and the lines; names that resolve to no person are listed apart under unresolved.
  • logbook/present.py, the "with" module: who was with the owner at a stay. present(stay, lines, identities) lists one entry per piece of evidence — a person id when the ref or name resolves through the record's resolution lines (RFC 0006; resolve.identities_from gives each ref its entity id and label), else the name or address as the source spelled it — with a confidence, a status and a reason: an attendee of a calendar entry whose span overlaps the stay (confirmed, 0.8 accepted, 0.6 tentative or unanswered, declined absent; attendee of <title>), a participant of a transcript recorded inside it (confirmed, 0.9, by email, phone, provider id, else the name against the labels; spoke in <title>), a note written inside it that says with <Name> (and <Name>; confirmed, 1.0; note says with <name>), and a face the library tagged in a photo taken inside it (provider_id ref <library>:<person id>; proposed, 0.5; face in <file>). A circle page is listed as a source and names nobody yet. company merges the evidence per person, confirmed first, with the sources, reasons and line ids.
  • logbook rollup countries|flights|nights [--year YYYY | --since YYYY-MM-DD --until YYYY-MM-DD] [--airports FILE] [--json] (logbook/rollup.py): the record summed up per year from one reading of the window, clipped to the days the owner's track covers (a day outside them is nothing, not a night in transit). countries: days per country per year from the overnight stay, in-transit nights and nights whose country is unknown listed separately, and the method printed with the numbers — logbook/countries.py: a place with a country (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, a new optional places.json field) whose radius holds the stay decides, else the nearest large airport within 300 km (the airports table) and its zone's country through the bundled logbook/tables/zones.csv (the zone database's public-domain zone.tab, regenerated by scripts/make_zones.py); coarse near borders and far from airports, and the module says so. flights: count, kilometres (great-circle between the airports table's coordinates), long-haul (over 3,500 km), unmeasured (an airport the table does not know), by evidence (tracked, inferred, declared), per year, from the flight lines standing (RFC 0013 rule 4), each flight listed with its route and km. nights: home, away and in-transit nights per year, nights aboard each asset, and the longest trip (the longest run of consecutive nights not at home); without a place of kind home every night is away and the rollup says so. Under --json every number carries the ids of the lines it came from: a stay by its first and last location line (one unbroken run), a flight by its line standing. Index.span(kind) gives the first and last local day with a line of a kind.
  • logbook places list|add|name|propose (and import-takeout, which moved beside them: the Google Maps saved-places importer now lives at logbook/adapters/takeout/places.py): the named places of the record. places.json (logbook/places.py) maps a name to {lat, lon, radius_m, kind, tags}, kind one of home, asset-berth, other (absent is other; the old three-field shape still reads); home regions are the places of kind home, and derive stays now marks each night home ("home": true in the JSON, · home in the table) when its stay is a home place or lies in one's radius. add <name> --lat --lon [--radius] [--kind] [--tags] edits the file only; name <lat,lon|stay-id> <name> adds the place and appends one note/v1 line, named <lat>,<lon> as <name>, so the naming is in the record. propose [--since] [--until] [--top N] [--json] is a reader: the owner's unnamed stays of the window (the whole record by default) grouped within 300 m and ranked by hours, each with its stay ids, the nearest known place and the distance, the asset it was aboard, the Google Timeline visits that overlap it when the record holds Takeout timeline lines (place id, semantic type, probability), a suggested name (the visit's semantic type, else aboard <asset>, else near <place> within 2 km), and under lines the ids of its first and last location line and the point count; --write asks for each name (Enter accepts the suggestion, s skips, q stops) and names the accepted ones as name does. Every segment of derive stays --json now carries a derived id (stay:owner:20260610T1000Z@59.9200,10.7400: kind, subject, start to the minute, centre) and lines (first and last location line id, points). logbook/reading.py is the one loader the readers share: a window's lines through the index, the settings, places and assets, the derived stays and nights, and the record's resolutions.
  • policy/import.json, {"disabled": [{"source", "reason"}]}: the sources the owner switched off. add, sync and import-backup skip a disabled source and say so (<name>: disabled (<reason>); skipped), --only or not, before anything is copied or any variable is asked for; logbook sources lists every adapter this build has, file and live, with enabled or disabled (<reason>), then any disabled name no adapter carries. Aliases resolve on both sides (books, health). init writes the empty list; a record without the file gets it on the first read. A malformed file exits 2 naming it and nothing is written. README: What never enters the record — demo, sample or placeholder data never enters the record; an adapter existing is not a decision to run it.
  • logbook places import-takeout <path> [--write]: Google Maps' saved and starred places — Takeout's Maps (your places)/Saved Places.json (GeoJSON, one Feature per place: the point, the title, the address and business name) and Saved/<list>.csv (Title,Note,URL,Comment, one list per file: Favourites, Want to go, Starred places, the owner's own; coordinates only when the url carries /@lat,lon or /search/lat,lon) — proposed as entries of places.json ({lat, lon, category, address?, note?}, category the list's name; stays.read_places ignores the extra keys) and written only with --write, new names added, an entry already there never changed, a place without coordinates listed and never geocoded (no network). Not lines: a saved place names coordinates, which is what derive stays reads from places.json. logbook/places.py.
  • logbook derive stays [--day YYYY-MM-DD | --since YYYY-MM-DD --until YYYY-MM-DD] [--subject ID] [--dry-run] [--json]: the first reader of the record. logbook/stays.py turns the window's location/v1 lines into stays, stops and moves, per subject (ADR 0018: the owner first, then each asset), and prints a table in local time (span, kind, place or coordinates, duration, what is attached, aboard) or one JSON object (window, settings, subjects, segments, nights, noise_points). The window runs from the first day's local midnight to 08:00 after the last, so the night is inside it. Points are clustered in time order against an anchor (the cluster's first point, or a named place's centre) within a radius, default 150 m; a single fix away and straight back is GPS noise, dropped and counted; a cluster under stop_min_s (3 min) is travel; the same place after a gap under merge_gap_s (10 min) is one stay, after a longer gap two stays with a move of no distance between them, printed as gap. A cluster is a stay when it lasts stay_min_s (20 min) or when anything is attached — an event, transcript, note, call, message or photo whose instant falls inside it, an end-bearing line when its span overlaps — evidence promotes (promoted: true), duration is the fallback; else a stop, kept and flagged nothing attached. Retracted lines never count; counts only, never a line's text. A move spans from one cluster's last point to the next's first: distance along the points between, duration, and a mode from the average speed (walk ≤ 7 km/h, car ≤ 130, train above, flight above 150 km/h or when a gap with no points starts and ends within 8 km of airports, airports: ["OSL", "BGO"]); the airports are the flights table (RFC 0013, flights.Airports), --airports FILE or LOGBOOK_AIRPORTS adding to it as for add flight. Aboard is derived, never written (ADR 0018 rule 3): the owner's stay is aboard an asset when the asset's positions in that span fall within the radius of the stay's centroid, a move when at least half the owner's points have an asset position within the radius at most aboard_window_s (5 min) away, a gap between two stays aboard the same asset; aboard a registered asset, or moving as one, the mode is the asset's kind (yacht → boat, aircraft → flight, car → car). The overnight stay of each day is the owner's stay with the longest overlap of the night window (night: ["22:00", "08:00"]) when that overlap reaches stay_min_s, else the day is in transit. Settings live in <root>/policy/stays.json, written with the defaults on the first real run and never rewritten (an edited file is honoured); --dry-run writes nothing, not even that, and says on stderr which settings apply. <root>/places.json ({"Home": {"lat": 59.91, "lon": 10.75, "radius_m": 120}}, the radius optional) names a stay and gives the place its own radius. assets.json is read through logbook.assets for the kinds and names. --subject <id> prints one asset's track, --subject owner the owner's; an id neither assets.json nor a line in the window names exits 2. Nothing is ever appended by this command. stays.derive(lines, settings, places, assets, tz) is the pure pass an engine calls without a folder. Tested on synthetic Oslo tracks: GPS noise, an outlier, a short and a long gap at home, a ten-minute cafe stop promoted by one photo, every evidence kind and a retracted message, walk and car by speed, a train to OSL and a gap to BGO as a flight, an overnight at home, a red-eye night in transit, a range of days, a yacht's synthetic AIS track with the owner aboard, the subject filter, an unknown subject, an empty day, and the same lines deriving twice to the same segments.
  • logbook stats --health [--json]: one row per local day from the health lines, read through the index (Index.of_kind, a streamed sweep of the files): sleep in hours (the asleep stages — asleep, core, deep, rem, never in_bed — of the night that ends on the day, summed per device, the longest device taken), steps (per quarter hour the larger device, summed), resting heart rate (the mean of the day's readings). Retracted lines are left out. Never a device, a zone or any other field; --json gives {"days": [...]}.
  • show folds one calendar entry that several sources carry into one row: two event/v1 lines with the same title (case and spacing aside), or naming the same flight in two spellings (Flight to Zürich (LX 561), Flug LX561 nach Zürich), starting within five minutes of each other, from different sources, print once, at the first one's time, with the source column naming them all (ics+ios-calendar). One calendar holding an entry twice is still two rows. The folded lines leave the day before the runs of location points are collapsed, so a repeat from a second calendar no longer breaks a run in two. Extends SPEC §3.2's run collapse on the reader's side; nothing about the record changes.
  • show prints a note/v1 line as its first line, then … (+N lines) when there are more (leading blank lines skipped); the whole text, as written, stays behind --raw. A day with three long meeting notes reads as three lines again.
  • show: a run of location points is one source and one subject (SPEC §3.2 as clarified); an asset's run is prefixed with its id, so a day at sea reads as the phone's points and the boat's.
  • Asset registry (ADR 0018): <root>/assets.json names the boats, aircraft and cars whose positions the record tracks as their own subjects, one entry {id, kind: yacht|aircraft|car, name, mmsi?, icao24?, registration?} each; logbook assets add <id> --kind --name [--mmsi] [--icao24] [--registration] registers one (an id, mmsi or icao24 belongs to one asset; an icao24 is stored lower-case; a bad entry is one line on stderr and exit 2) and logbook assets list prints them. A setting of the record, outside the chain, read through logbook.assets; unknown keys of the file are preserved.
  • logbook add flight "LX 561 NCE ZRH 2026-09-27 pilot 07:05-08:20 A320 ZZ-ABC": the owner's word as a manual flight/v1 line, evidence declared — designator, origin, destination, date, then optionally the role (default passenger), a departure and arrival clock (local at each airport, recorded as actual; an arrival before the departure is the next local day), an aircraft type and a registration. A sentence that starts flight but not with a designator is still a note; one that starts with a designator and does not parse exits 2 with the format. A declared flight the record already holds is merged into it (the role wins) and the console says so.
  • logbook infer flights [--since DAY] [--until DAY] [--airports FILE] [--dry-run]: flight/v1 lines, source flight-inference, evidence inferred, from the record's own evidence: a calendar entry (event/v1, its last version standing, not cancelled) whose title names a flight (LX 561, Flight to Zurich (LX 561); an airline the table does not know needs the word "flight" or ✈), plus a silence of twenty minutes or more in the location points around it that starts within 8 km of one airport and ends within 8 km of another; the gap's edges are the actual times, the entry's span the scheduled ones, the airports the gap's; a route in the title (OSL-ZRH) picks between candidate gaps, else the longest wins. An entry without such a gap is a plan and produces nothing (counted). extra.event and extra.gap name the entry and the two points. A re-run appends nothing; a flight Flighty already tracked gets the inference attached as an observation.
  • show prints a flight as XY 561 OSL → ZRH, arrives 09:24, Airbus A320 LN-XYA, tracked, as pilot and a flight line another flight line superseded as superseded by #N. Index.by_kind(kind, first_day, last_day) and Index.superseded(kind) (from the supersedes column, no rebuild). adapters.named resolves the alias flights → flighty. Tests: the tables (every zone loads), the grammar, the merge in every order, the adapter on a synthetic export (Oslo persona, airline XY), the inference on synthetic tracks around Oslo and Zürich airports, the CLI end to end.
  • verify streams the record (#28): Logbook.lines() is now a merge of the month files — every file open at once, one parsed line from each in a heap keyed by seq, the smallest yielded and its file read on — so memory is one line per month file however long the record; the whole-log export streams the same way. On a synthetic record of 3,000,000 lines over 120 month files, verify went from 72 s and 4.7 GB peak RSS to 54 s and 23 MB, and export of the whole log from 26 s and 6.5 GB to 23 s and 29 MB. The writer keeps every file in seq order and the merge relies on it; a file that is not (SPEC §3 orders by seq wherever a line was found, so such a record can still be valid) raises UnsortedFile, and verify and the whole-log export then read again through the two-pass sorted read migrate uses, sixteen bytes a line. verify --progress prints one line per month file on stderr as its last line is checked — files finish in the order of their last seq, so a backfilled month finishes early — and stdout stays the one line it always was, byte for byte. verify still never opens the index.
  • Dedupe without the log in memory (#29): append_many has deduped through the index since ADR 0007 — one SELECT per 10,000-draft batch against the (source, raw_id) index, the in-memory set only the batch's own keys, the index extended at every checkpoint so nothing is ever appended past it — and the issue's premise no longer held; this closes it with the measurement: 100,000 drafts already in a 3,000,000-line record are deduped in two to three seconds at 41 MB peak RSS, the same before and after. show and export --day read only the lines the index locates (checked by a test that fails if either lists or scans the month files). Two slow tests (LOGBOOK_SLOW=1) build the 3,000,000-line record in a temporary folder and assert that verify's peak RSS on it is within 48 MB of a 1,000,000-line record's and that the dedupe stays under 256 MB, each measured in a process of its own.
  • index.sqlite schema 3: the media column stats counts also reads a payload.content reference (RFC 0004), so transcripts count as attachments; an existing index is rebuilt once, by the first reader. show prints a transcript as <title> — <participants>; <turns>, <length>, a participant by the resolution of its email when one exists, never the text. logbook add passes store (the attachment store), source, tier and at to an adapter whose run takes them, and refuses --source/--tier for one that does not.
  • export crossing --to <destination> --since <RFC3339|last> [--until <RFC3339>] [--tier 1|1,2|1,2,3] [--kinds a,b] [--out <dir>] [--dry-run] (#77): one crossing-package/v1 bundle (RFC 0005) for a named circle member, the lines of the half-open window [since, until) verbatim in entries.jsonl, read through the index and never rewritten; attachments/<sha256> copies of every SPEC §1.1 file the store holds (hashed on the way; a missing one stays a reference and is counted); resolution.jsonl with every resolution line the exported refs resolve through, alias hops included (RFC 0006), nothing else from outside the window; manifest.json with logbook_head, covers, recipient, tiers, counts (logged, crossed, held back, per tier, per kind, resolutions, attachments), blobs, the digest of each file, the tool version, a review list of every tier-2 line when tier 2 crosses and a tier3 warning when tier 3 does. The ceiling per destination lives in <root>/policy/crossing.json (ADR 0016), {"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}} by default, written by init and by the first export; a request above it, or to a destination the file does not name, exits 2 naming the file; tier 3 needs both the file and an explicit --tier 1,2,3, and the console says so loudly. Every real export appends one tier-1 crossing/v1 line, source logbook (RFC 0011): destination, window, counts, policy in force, logbook_head, and package_sha256, the digest of manifest.json; then records the window end per destination in <root>/exports/crossing.json, which --since last reads (the first run without it is refused with the flag to pass). --dry-run prints the counts per kind and tier, the attachment bytes and the policy that would apply and writes nothing. A retracted line is held back. Index.window locates a window by at; resolve.standing and resolve.walk expose the last-line-standing map and the alias walk labels was built on.
  • logbook stats [--json]: one screen of what a record holds, read through the index in one SELECT per table and nothing from the files: format and head; lines, first and last at; lines per kind with first and last local day and distinct sources; lines per source; lines per local year as a bar of one character per ~1% of the busiest year; retractions and the lines they hide; resolution lines and the entities they mint; attachments referenced under payload.media or extra.media (SPEC §1.1) and how many are present under attachments/; and what the run took. Numbers, kinds, sources and dates only, never payload content. index.sqlite schema 2 adds the supersedes, entity and media columns it counts; an existing index is rebuilt once, by the first reader.

docs.title: Fixes and housekeeping
docs.text:
• verify --progress reports the month files in path order, each as file n of N: <path>: ... (#120, fixes #101). The merge in Logbook.lines() finishes a small file long before a large earlier one, so the lines came out in heap-exhaustion order and a reader could not tell how far the run was; a file that finishes early is now held until every earlier path has, and the counter runs 1, 2, … N.
  • show no longer fails on an event whose attendee is a string, the shape before RFC 0009: SPEC §3.2 reads it as an email ref, named through the record's resolution lines like any other, and anything else is printed as it is (SPEC §5: a reader never fails on a payload it cannot interpret). The conformance sample's first day showed it. logbook/present.py no longer raises a SyntaxWarning for an escaped asterisk in its docstring.
  • Scrub: init prints the record as ~/Logbook when it is under the home directory, never the expanded path, and docs/demo.gif is re-recorded from a throwaway home (the old one showed a real user name); the example flight sentence and the Flighty fixture carry the unassigned registration ZZ-ABC instead of a real airline's; the Withings profile ids, the Reminders store names and the Norwegian numbers outside the persona's +47 9000 000x block in the fixtures are re-patterned. Nothing in the tree matched the owner's private identifier list.
  • Tests no longer see the shell's LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD: tests/conftest.py clears it beside LOGBOOK_HOME and the home directory.
  • infer flights missed every flight of a tracker that keeps logging in the air. The search wanted a silence of twenty minutes between a point at one airport and a point at another; a phone that logs the take-off roll and the climb starts its silence from a point seven kilometres up, near no airport, and one that logs the whole flight is never silent at all, so neither was a flight. Now the search is for a leg: the last point within 8 km of one airport, then the first point within 8 km of a different one, every point between them near no airport, at least twenty minutes apart (flights.MIN_LEG, was MIN_GAP); the leg's two points are the actual times and extra.gap as before, silence in between is usual but not required. Airports.nearest looks up the nine one-degree cells around a point (CELL_KM) so every point of a day can be placed, not only a gap's edges. "Flug" counts as a flight word beside "flight" and ✈ (Flug XY561 nach Zürich). Four calendar entries for one flight (two calendars, two spellings) gave four identical inferences: the dry run said four flights and the real run wrote one and called the other three "already in the record". flights.reconcile now drops a draft that repeats an observation earlier in the same stream, and the dry run counts the observations the record already holds the way the real run does, so both say 1 flight from 4 calendar entries. The skip phrase reads calendar flights the location points do not confirm. Found on a real record's September; reproduced on synthetic tracks around Oslo and Zürich airports.
  • granola: a note Granola made without recording (one empty turn from an instant to the same instant, duration_s 0) was still logged as a transcript/v1 line with an empty transcript stored under it. Now such a note yields only its summary as the note/v1 line, raw_id granola:<note id>:summary as ever, extra.derived_from set only when the record already holds a transcript for the note (else left out, derived_from_raw_id still names it), nothing stored, and the skip counted as without a recording. granola.recorded(line, segments) is the rule: a segment with words, or a span above zero seconds. Tested with a synthetic note carrying one empty segment.
  • import-backup: the Safari step reported safari: History.db not found on every encrypted backup. The source was registered under AppDomain-com.apple.mobilesafari; the phone backs the file up in HomeDomain at Library/Safari/History.db, and that is where ios_backup.EXTRAS now looks. A store is resolved through the Files table of Manifest.db by domain and relativePath, never by a fixed fileID; the test plants a synthetic row whose fileID is not the SHA-1 a backup would give it and copies the file from where that row points. The encrypted-backup fixture, which had copied the wrong domain, is corrected.
  • import-backup: a copy is checked against the stored blob, not the manifest's Size. An iOS 26.5 backup records a file's size on the phone (Size) while the blob it stores is another size, so the first file stopped the import with copied 29,650,944 bytes, the backup has 35,745,792 although the decryption was exact (blob 29,650,960 = plaintext + 16 bytes of PKCS#7 padding). Now a decrypted copy must equal the blob's length less the padding stripped (ios_backup_crypto.decrypt_file returns Decrypted(written, padding) and strips valid padding before it honours Size; a blob whose last block is not padding fails), a plain copy must equal the blob byte for byte (the manifest's Size is now read for an unencrypted backup too), and a copy that matches the blob but not Size is one warning: line naming the file and both sizes, never an error. copies.json records the copy's real bytes and, per copy, that warning. Plan.copied is a list of ios_backup.Copy.
  • Repository hygiene: scripts/check_pii.py is a stdlib-only pre-commit hook that greps every added line of the staged diff for the owner's personal identifiers and fails the commit on a match, printing the file and line but never the text. The identifiers never enter the repository: the hook reads one case-insensitive regex per line from the file LOGBOOK_PII_PATTERNS names (default ~/.config/logbook/pii-patterns); without the file it prints one warning and passes, so CI and other checkouts are unaffected. Tested against a temporary patterns file of synthetic values only. CLAUDE.md gains the commit routine (author identity, -s -S, git log -1 --format='%G?' → G, how to create the patterns file) and the release routine (grep __version__ on the tagged commit before git tag -s).
  • imessage: an attachment row with no filename is only extra.media_missing; extra.media is no longer written with a media_type and no path, so it always carries local_path as its docstring and RFC 0008's media rule say, the fix #74 gave whatsapp (its media_kind still comes from the mime type). The property test fixes itself to the adapter (#75): its date floor is computed from APPLE_EPOCH + EARLIEST_DATE (2010-07-05T05:20:00Z, not the 7th); the media rule holds in the first slot and under extra.more_media; a sender may carry the optional name RFC 0008 added (#59), never blank, which the test's store now grows a display_name column to exercise.
  • whatsapp: a media row with no ZMEDIALOCALPATH is only extra.media_missing; extra.media is no longer written with a title and no path, so it always carries local_path as its docstring and RFC 0008's media rule say. The property test fixes itself to the adapter (#66): its date floor is computed from APPLE_EPOCH + EARLIEST_DATE (2010-07-05T05:20:00Z, not the 7th), and a sender may carry the optional name RFC 0008 added (#59), never blank.
  • CI: a cross-impl job on every pull request and push to main builds the independent TypeScript implementation (bighydro/logbook-ts) at its main, checks that its verify prints the head in conformance/expected.json on conformance/sample-logbook, then appends one note to a copy of the sample with the Python CLI and verifies the copy with the TypeScript CLI: the two implementations must agree on a record the other wrote.

docs.title: 0.4.1 — 2026-09-25
docs.text: • Documentation fix; no code behaviour change: the example phone number in README, adapters/phone.py and the ios-contacts tests is now the UK fictional-range number 07700 900123 (dial prefix 44), never a real one. CLAUDE.md hard rule: example phone numbers, emails and addresses come only from reserved fictional ranges.

docs.title: 0.4.0 — 2026-09-21
docs.text:
• SPEC §1.1 (ADR 0015): the content-addressed attachment store, attachments/<sha256>, optional, write-once, never pruned, outside the hash chain; the { sha256, path, bytes, media_type } reference shape that RFCs 0004, 0005, 0008 and 0010 point at. No format bump; nothing implemented yet.
  • SPEC clarifications, no format bump, no hash change: GENESIS named; month-file placement is a writer MUST, not a validity condition; every envelope field present and end null, never absent; timestamps UTC with Z, fractional seconds hashed verbatim; seq decimal unpadded and hex lowercase in the pre-image; the verifier checks §2 as well as the chain; duplicate keys and duplicate seq are invalid; only the canonical form is hashed; unknown keys in logbook.json are preserved; the write order (lines, then logbook.json, then the index). §6 and conformance/README.md now state the same tamper-and-delete condition. Found by the clean-room TypeScript implementation.
  • The reference is as strict as SPEC §2–3 (#47), no hash change: verify names any missing envelope field (end is null, never absent; schema/observation.schema.json now requires it); a line with a duplicate JSON key, at any depth, is invalid on read; writers normalise at/end/recorded_at to UTC with a literal Z (an offset is converted, a stamp with no zone is refused); verify reports a timestamp with a numeric offset as a WARNING in this release — the record stays valid, exit 0 — and the next release makes it an error; append/append_many fsync the month files before logbook.json is saved.
  • ios-contacts file adapter: an iPhone's AddressBook.sqlitedb (also the hashed file in an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup) → resolution/v1 (RFC 0006), one line per phone number and email address, minting one UUIDv7 per contact as person or company — how a record gets its people (ADR 0013.2). Opened read-only and immutable; refs are deduped on the normalised value so a later backup appends nothing already resolved; LOGBOOK_DIAL_PREFIX completes numbers saved without a country code, dropping one national trunk 0. logbook add now reports every count an adapter tallies, not only the location ones.
  • whatsapp file adapter: an iPhone's WhatsApp ChatStorage.sqlite (also the hashed file in an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup) → message/v1 (RFC 0008), one line per message: chat (direct or group; broadcast lists are groups; status chats skipped), sender as a source-native phone or handle ref through the new shared adapters/phone.py (so a WhatsApp number and an address-book number are the same ref), text, media_kind. raw_id is <chat jid>:<stanza id> so a later backup appends nothing already logged. Media v1 rule: files are never copied into the record; a file present under Message/ is hashed into extra.media (sha256, bytes, local_path) for a later attach pass, a missing one is extra.media_missing; payload.media is never set (the §1.1 store is not built yet); LOGBOOK_WHATSAPP_HASH_MEDIA=0 skips the hashing. Streams the store through one cursor, built for a million rows. logbook add now also reports what an adapter noted without skipping (media hashed or missing, rows keyed by row id).
  • imessage file adapter: an iPhone's Messages sms.db (also the hashed file in an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup) and the chat.db macOS keeps under ~/Library/Messages → message/v1 (RFC 0008), one line per message: chat (direct or group), sender as a source-native phone, email or handle ref through the shared adapters/phone.py, text, reply_to, media_kind, extra.service. raw_id is the message guid, so a later backup appends nothing already logged. A body that iOS 16+ keeps only in attributedBody (an NSArchiver typedstream) is decoded by a stdlib-only reader; tapbacks and group events are skipped and counted (rule 1); a date in seconds or nanoseconds since 2001 is read either way. Media v1 rule as for WhatsApp: no file is copied and payload.media is never set; a file present under Attachments/ beside the database is hashed into extra.media, a missing one is extra.media_missing, further attachments go under extra.more_media; LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_HASH_MEDIA=0 skips the hashing. One streamed SELECT, opened read-only and immutable.
  • ios-notes file adapter: an iPhone's Apple Notes NoteStore.sqlite (also the hashed file in an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup) → note/v1 (RFC 0010), one line per note at its creation time: text decoded from the gzip+protobuf note archive by a stdlib-only walker (field path 2 → 3 → 2), falling back to the snippet when the archive will not decode; title, folder, modified_at; raw_id is <identifier>@<modified_at> so an edited note is a new line and an unchanged one appends nothing. Password-protected notes are skipped (the body is encrypted); notes marked for deletion are logged with extra.deleted; a note with no recoverable text or no usable creation date is skipped. Checklist markers (RFC 0010 rule 3) are not interpreted yet. Opened read-only and immutable, streamed through one cursor.
  • ios-calendar file adapter: an iPhone's Calendar.sqlitedb (also the hashed file in an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup) → event/v1 (RFC 0009), one line per stored entry: span in UTC with the entry's own zone, calendar, title, notes, location (coordinates under extra.location), organizer and attendees as email refs with their responses, status. A recurring master carries its rule as RRULE text and a detached occurrence carries recurrence_of; occurrences are never expanded. raw_id is <uid>@<last modified> (rule 5), so an edited entry is a new line next time. Placeholder rows (a start before 1900, such as 1601) and rows with no start are skipped and counted. supersedes is never set on import; readers join an edited entry's lines on the bare uid. Every column beyond the start is optional, for other iOS versions. logbook add now passes the record's timezone to an adapter whose run takes timezone, so a floating all-day entry lands at local midnight.
  • show prints people by name from the record's own resolution lines (RFC 0006): the sender of a message, the organizer and attendees of an event. Index.resolutions() yields every resolution line in chain order (no schema change, no rebuild); logbook/resolve.py builds one {(ref.kind, ref.value): label} map per invocation, skipping retracted lines and the line a later resolution supersedes, the last one standing winning for a ref (rule 4). A chat is not an entity: an unnamed group prints its chat.id as the source gave it. show --raw prints every ref unchanged. show still only reads.
  • RFC 0008: sender gains an optional name, the sender's display name as the source shows it (a WhatsApp push name or group-member contact name; iMessage fills it only from a store whose handle table has a display_name column), never a resolution. show falls back to it when no resolution names the sender, before the direct chat's own name and the raw ref; --raw ignores it.
  • Tests never see the shell's LOGBOOK_HOME or home directory (HOME, USERPROFILE): an autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py pins both to a temporary folder for every test, so a test can never open the real record at ~/Logbook. Never remove it (CLAUDE.md).

docs.title: 0.3.0 — 2026-09-15
docs.text:
• BREAKING: records created by 0.1.0 or 0.2.0 must run logbook migrate once before any other command will read or write them (SPEC §3.1).
  • Format logbook/0.2 (SPEC §3.1, ADR 0014): canonical_json is now RFC 8785 exactly (UTF-16 key order, ECMAScript float layout; tested against the RFC's vectors). 0.1 hashed floats such as 0.0, 120.0 and 1e-06 differently, so verify and every writer refuse a 0.1 record; logbook migrate recomputes prev/hash in seq order, keeps everything else, records lineage in logbook.json, appends one migration/v1 line, keeps the 0.1 files at logbook-0.1/. The conformance sample is 0.2.
  • index.sqlite: a disposable SQLite locator of the files (ADR 0001, 0007) — logbook index builds it in one streaming pass; show, retract, export --day/--days and add/sync dedupe go through it and rebuild it when it is missing or stale; append/append_many extend it at each checkpoint; verify and whole-log export never read it. show now lists a local day (the owner's timezone) with local clock times, as export --day always did.
  • sync <source> [--since RFC3339] [--dry-run] pulls from a live source through the new live-adapter contract (configure/pull) and keeps its watermark in state/; first live adapter: immich → photo/v1 (RFC 0002), stdlib urllib only.

docs.title: 0.2.0 — 2026-09-15
docs.text:
• Docs site (MkDocs Material) deployed from main; reproducible demo tape.
  • Package published as openlogbook; the command is logbook.
  • init and find refuse a code checkout (#12).
  • export --day DATE / --days FROM TO write day-package/v1 directories (ADR 0013 §4); export/ is ignored.
  • add takes several paths (logbook add a.json b.json some/dir); a path that does not exist is an error (exit 2), never a note.
  • retract SEQ "reason" writes a retraction/v1 line that supersedes SEQ (SPEC §3); show hides the retracted line behind a marker, export --day keeps it and adds retracted_by.
  • export --days reads the log once for the whole range instead of once per day.

• Format v0.1: folder layout, envelope, hash chain, tiers, conformance rule.
  • CLI: init, add (text or JSONL), show, verify, export.
  • Conformance fixture with expected head.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Code is Apache-2.0. Contributions to SPEC.md are CC0. Read SPEC.md and ARCHITECTURE.md first: the record's rules are there, and a change that needs to break one is wrong.

There is one way to do each thing here. Where this page and a habit disagree, this page wins.

docs.title: Set up once
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bighydro/logbook && cd logbook
uv sync --group dev                       # Python 3.12, every dependency, the dev tools
uv run pre-commit install                 # ruff, gitleaks, the PII check, on every commit
git config gpg.format ssh && git config user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub   # or your GPG key

Register the signing key on GitHub (how) so the pull request shows Verified. Then create ~/.config/logbook/pii-patterns, one case-insensitive regular expression per line for your own identifiers (your names, numbers, addresses, account ids, the names of your contacts). The pre-commit hook scripts/check_pii.py greps every added line against it and stops you before CI does. The file is never committed, printed or pasted anywhere.

docs.title: Do one change
docs.text:
1. Pick or open one issue. The pull request closes it and nothing else. A second change is a second branch.
  2. One branch, one worktree, one session. git worktree add ../logbook-<issue> -b <branch>, then uv sync --group dev and uv run pre-commit install in it, since each worktree has its own .venv and hooks. Work there and nowhere else, never check out another branch in it, and never run anything against a real record: tests/conftest.py pins LOGBOOK_HOME and the home directory to a temp dir, and nothing unsets that.
  3. Test first. Write the failing test, run it, implement, run it again: 
    uv run pytest tests/test_<area>.py       # the test you wrote
uv run pytest -n auto                    # the whole suite, as CI runs it
uv run ruff check --fix . && uv run mypy logbook
  4. Commit after each step, signed and signed off. git commit -s -S, then git log -1 --format='%G?' prints G. Anything else means unsigned; fix it before pushing. Conventional commit prefixes: feat:, fix:, spec:, docs:, adapter:.
  5. Add a changelog fragment, never a line in CHANGELOG.md. changelog.d/<short-slug>.md holds one or a few - lines in the changelog's own wording, optionally under ### Added, ### Fixed or another heading the changelog already uses (changelog.d/README.md). A change with nothing to tell the user gets the no-changelog label on its pull request instead.
  6. Push and open the pull request against main. Fill in the template. CI must be green before review; a first-time contributor's workflows wait until a maintainer approves them, which is GitHub's default and not a judgement on the change.
  7. When it merges, git worktree remove ../logbook-<issue> and delete the branch.

docs.title: The rules every pull request keeps
docs.text:
• Nothing real enters the tree. Not a record, not an export, not a screenshot, not a line in a pull request description. Every fixture, test, example and docs page uses the sample person, who lives in Oslo and does not exist, and her circle (docs/try-it.md, Who). Phone numbers come from the UK's fictional block 07700 900xxx or the persona's +47 9000 000x block already in the fixtures. Email addresses are at example.org. Addresses, places, businesses, the airline XY, the aircraft ZZ-ABC, the yachts Solvind and Nordlys on the unassigned MMSI 999000001 are invented. An identifier that looks like a service's own (a JID, a Matrix event id, a bank transaction id) is re-patterned by hand, never copied from a real export. A fixture is written by hand or generated by code checked in beside it (logbook/demo.py, conformance/make_sample.py).
  • Scrub, then check the scrub. A fixture that started life as your own export is swapped identifier by identifier for ones from the reserved ranges, so it still reads as a record; a blanked field is a fixture that no longer tests what it tested. The check is the pre-commit hook, or /usr/bin/grep or Python's re by hand, never bare grep: on a Mac where grep is ugrep a pattern that matches nothing proves nothing. Checks print counts only. Record demos from a throwaway home directory; a prompt can leak what a file does not.
  • The log is written only through Logbook.append. No code path updates or deletes a line. A correction is a new line that retracts an old one.
  • No network on an adapter's default path, no write to any source. An adapter that reads an app's own store confirms the columns it needs with PRAGMA table_info first and tolerates drift: a column it does not need may be missing or renamed and the rows still read; a table it needs that is absent is a counted skip or one clear error naming the store, never a traceback.
  • The envelope (SPEC §2 and §3) changes only with a spec version bump, a regenerated conformance fixture and an ADR in docs/adr/.
  • Windows runs the tests too, and it has caught a bug in every pull request that forgot it. Paths through pathlib, never as strings; zoneinfo needs tzdata there; a subprocess is read with encoding="utf-8", never text=True; every SQLite connection and file is closed before an unlink; digests are taken over the bytes written with write_bytes, never over the string formatted; a test that needs a real shell skips on win32; a test that needs its own home directory monkeypatches Path.home or sets both HOME and USERPROFILE. Filesystems on macOS and Windows are case-insensitive, so files are never told apart by case.

docs.title: Write an adapter
docs.text:
The easiest and most useful thing to build is an adapter for the export you already have. The ones wanted, with their export formats, profiles and tiers, are in the bounty list; the ones marked good first adapter are a few hours each.

  1. Copy adapters/template/ to logbook/contrib/adapters/<source>.py with its tests and tests/fixtures/<source>/.
  2. Put a small, synthetic export in the fixture folder. Never real data, not even yours.
  3. Write NAME, sniff(path) -> bool and run(input_path, since) yielding observations with a payload.schema from an existing RFC. A new shape is a new RFC first (below).
  4. Register the module once, in pyproject.toml under [project.entry-points."logbook.adapters"], where logbook add should try it (the order is find's precedence); tests/test_adapter_registry.py fails on a module that is not there. Add a page under docs/adapters/ when the source needs explaining.
  5. Run the tests; the expected output is generated on the first run and checked in.
  6. Open the pull request as adapter: <source>.

A source that has both an export and a live API is one adapter with one mapping: backfill and live share it, so the same observation arrives once, with one shape and one raw_id, whichever way it came (ADR 0017).

docs.title: Propose a profile or a spec change
docs.text: A payload profile or a change to SPEC.md is an RFC: open an issue with the RFC template, then a pull request adding rfcs/NNNN-<name>.md with a JSON Schema, one synthetic example line and the backwards-compatibility note. Two weeks of comment; the captain merges or declines with reasons (GOVERNANCE.md). A change to the envelope is a major version and ships with a migration tool.

docs.title: The clean-room rule for logbook-ts
docs.text: logbook-ts exists to prove that SPEC.md is enough to implement the format (SPEC §6: two independent implementations must agree before 1.0 is frozen). It proves that only while it stays independent. A contributor to logbook-ts works from SPEC.md, the RFCs and conformance/, never from this repository's source, tests or diffs; if you had to read the Python to understand a rule, the rule is underspecified, so file that against the spec instead of carrying the answer across. Nothing is ported in either direction: a fix found by one implementation becomes a spec question, is resolved in SPEC.md with a changelog line naming the finder, and only then is implemented on each side from the spec's words. Keep the two in separate checkouts and separate sessions; an agent that has one open does not open the other.

docs.title: Slow tests
docs.text:
The suite runs in parallel (uv run pytest -n auto) and a pull request's CI should finish in minutes, so a test is marked by how long it takes. No marker: under about five seconds, run on every push and pull request. @pytest.mark.slow: over about five seconds and still a plain correctness test, skipped unless LOGBOOK_SLOW=1, which CI sets on a push to main and nightly; run them once before opening a pull request with LOGBOOK_SLOW=1 uv run pytest -n auto -m slow. @pytest.mark.stress: the generated millions-of-lines tests with timing and memory assertions, skipped unless LOGBOOK_STRESS=1 and never run in CI. A test owns nothing but its tmp_path: no fixed port, no file in the working tree, no order it relies on.

Before a rename merges, run the fuzz readers. A pull request that renames a command or changes a reader's output gets one run of LOGBOOK_SLOW=1 uv run pytest tests/test_fuzz_readers.py before it merges, and ticks the box in the template. Those tests are slow-tier, so the pull-request CI tier skips them and a regression only shows on the push to main after the merge: #215 (the 22-command rename) turned main red that way on 4 October 2026, and #217 fixed it forward.

docs.title: What CI checks
docs.text: Every pull request and every push to main: ruff and mypy; the suite on Linux, macOS and Windows with Python 3.12 and 3.13; the conformance rule (logbook verify on conformance/sample-logbook prints the head in conformance/expected.json); the Nix and Docker builds; cross-impl, which builds logbook-ts at its main, checks that it prints the same head on the sample, appends one note to a copy with this CLI and verifies the copy with that one; and changelog, which fails a pull request that edits CHANGELOG.md or adds no fragment unless it carries the no-changelog label.

docs.title: Where does my code go
docs.text:
One package, three tiers (ARCHITECTURE.md; logbook/layout.py declares them, tests/test_layout.py holds the tree to it):

  • logbook/core/ — the format and what SPEC.md freezes with it: the chain, the record, the index, the attachment store, the tiers, and a reader whose JSON a second implementation is compared on (§6.1). A change here is a spec change until proven otherwise.
  • logbook/contrib/ — an adapter (contrib/adapters/<source>.py, one module per source, registered once in pyproject.toml; BUILT_IN is generated from that table), an import or sync, an export, or a derived reader whose output is a reader's own. Imports core and contrib, never labs.
  • logbook/labs/ — anything that runs a model, or is still an experiment. Imported only when its command runs.
  • logbook/commands/ — the command itself: <name>_arguments(sub) and cmd_<name>(a) in the family's module, a line in parser.py; an adapter or a labs module imported inside the function, so logbook --help stays cheap.
  • A module that moves keeps its old import path for one minor version (layout.MOVED, docs/migration-0.6.md).

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
Captain. A ship has one captain and the captain signs the log. bighydro writes the specification, merges, releases, and writes the letters. bighydro is a pen name and stays one; the project is judged by its documents and its two implementations, not by its author.

What changes how. - The envelope (SPEC §1–3) changes only by major version, with a migration tool, after both implementations pass the new fixture. - A payload profile changes through an RFC in rfcs/: a pull request with the schema, one synthetic fixture and the readers it affects; two weeks of public comment; a second implementation that emits or reads it; merge. A frozen profile (v1.0) changes only by a new version alongside the old. - Architecture decisions are ADRs in docs/adr/. Everything else is a pull request with a changelog fragment.

Two implementations. No version of the format is final until two independent implementations agree on the conformance fixture for every reader SPEC §6.1 names. Disagreement is a specification bug until proven otherwise.

Merging. Signed commits only. Synthetic data only. Readers open no network connection, and CI checks it. A pull request that touches the format needs one review from someone other than its author; today that is often a reviewing agent, and we say so.

Disagreement. Decisions are made in public issues. When a contributor and the captain disagree, the captain decides and writes down why in the issue. A decision can be reopened by a new argument, never by repetition.

Succession. If the captain is silent for twelve months, the most recent two contributors with merged format changes may jointly tag a release and amend this file. When the project has three officers of the watch, this file is replaced by a charter and the specification moves to a foundation that no one involved controls. That is the intention from the first day, written here so that it can be held against us.

docs.title: Lore — where the logbook comes from
docs.text: A project needs to know its ancestors. Logbook has two lines of descent, human and computational, and they turn out to be the same line.

docs.title: I. The human logbook
docs.text:
The knot and the board. In the 1500s a sailor measured a ship's speed by throwing a flat wooden board — the log — over the stern on a line knotted at fixed intervals, and counting how many knots ran out while a small sandglass emptied. Speed at sea is still given in knots because of that board. The readings were entered in a book beside the helm: the log-book. Course, speed, wind, weather, position, every few hours, in ink, in order, initialled by the officer of the watch. Within a century "logbook" meant the whole record of a voyage: who came aboard, who died, what was sighted, what was decided. It was never written for an audience. It was written because things happened, and because later someone would need to know what actually occurred.

Truth by construction. A ship's log is admissible in court. Entries are made at the time, in sequence, in a bound book with numbered pages; an error is struck through with a single line so the original stays legible, and the correction is initialled. Nothing is erased. Nothing is written later and backdated. Three rules — append only, corrections as new entries, never delete — that are four hundred years older than any database and identical to the ones this project enforces.

The voyages we know only because someone kept the book. Antonio Pigafetta kept the diary of Magellan's circumnavigation (1519–22); only eighteen men came home, and most of what we know of the first voyage around the earth is his book. James Cook's journals fixed the coastlines of the Pacific. Charles Darwin kept a diary aboard Beagle for five years (1831–36); On the Origin of Species grew out of those notebooks, twenty years later, because he could reread what he had actually seen rather than what he remembered seeing. Robert Falcon Scott's last diary was found beside his body in the Antarctic in 1912; Shackleton's men kept theirs on the ice for two years and every one of them came home. Lighthouse keepers, weather stations, station masters, mine foremen: for three centuries the ordinary world was run by people making dated entries in ruled books, and the climate scientists of our own century now reconstruct the weather of the 1800s from ships' logs, because those pages are the only instruments that were there.

The captain's logbook and the pilot's. Every pilot alive keeps a logbook. It is a legal document: date, aircraft, route, hours, landings, who was in command. A licence is granted on the strength of it and can be lost over it. It is the one place where a pilot's life in the air is true, and pilots are sentimental about theirs in a way they are about nothing else. The captain's log — the phrase is now a joke from television — was the same thing at sea: the commander's own record, in the first person, of what was decided and why.

The private book. Beside the official log there was always another book. Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations for no reader but himself; the Greek title is simply "to himself". Samuel Pepys kept a diary in shorthand for nine years (1660–69) and recorded the plague, the Great Fire, and his own small vanities with equal care; nobody read it for a century and a half. Benjamin Franklin ruled a small book into thirteen virtues and marked each evening's faults with a dot — the first self-tracker. Leonardo's notebooks, Thoreau's journal, the commonplace books in which people for centuries copied what they wanted to keep: none of these were feeds. They were written by one person, for that person, to be reread.

The captain of my soul. William Ernest Henley wrote Invictus in 1875 from a hospital bed, after losing a foot to tuberculosis of the bone:

I am the master of my fate, I am the captain of my soul.

The poem is a claim of ownership over one's own voyage. A logbook is the instrument that makes the claim true: you cannot be the captain of a voyage no one recorded.

docs.title: II. The computational logbook
docs.text:
Same word, same object. When engineers needed a name for an ordered, append-only, timestamped record of what a machine had done, they took the sailor's word. Operating systems have written log files since the 1960s; Unix syslog (Eric Allman, 1980s) gave every program a common place to write a dated line. The metaphor was exact: something happened, write it down, in order, don't go back.

The log as the truth. Database engineers discovered that the log was not a byproduct of the database — it was the database. The write-ahead log (formalised in the ARIES papers, C. Mohan and colleagues, 1992) writes every change to an append-only file before touching the tables, so that after a crash the tables can be rebuilt from the log, but the log can never be rebuilt from the tables. Journaling filesystems did the same for disks. Leslie Lamport's Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events (1978) showed that in a distributed system the only thing that can be agreed on is an order of events — a log. Jay Kreps's essay The Log (LinkedIn, 2013), which led to Apache Kafka, says it in one sentence: the log is the source of truth; every table, index, cache and view is a derived, disposable projection of it. This project's first principle — the log is immutable, moments are disposable, notes are sacred — is that sentence applied to a life.

Making the log unforgeable. Ralph Merkle (1979) showed how to hash a tree of records so that changing any leaf changes the root. Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta (1991) chained timestamped documents by hashing each one together with the previous — a linked hash chain, built so that no one, not even the keeper, could later alter a page without breaking every page after it. Git (2005) made every commit a hash of its content and its parent, so that a repository's history is verifiable by anyone who holds it. Bitcoin (2008) put the same chain in public. Logbook uses the 1991 version: one person's private chain, verifiable by that person, needing no one else's agreement. The ship's log struck a line through errors and initialled the page; the hash chain is the initial.

The dream of a machine that remembers for you. Vannevar Bush described the memex in 1945 — a desk that stores everything a person reads and the trails between them. Ted Nelson's Xanadu, Douglas Engelbart's augmentation, and the hypertext that became the web all descend from it. Steve Mann wore a camera and computer through the 1990s, logging his life continuously. Gordon Bell at Microsoft spent the 2000s on MyLifeBits, scanning and recording everything he did, and wrote Total Recall (2009) about it. The Quantified Self movement (Gary Wolf and Kevin Kelly, 2007) turned self-tracking into a practice. Every one of these got the record right and left the recount and the circle unbuilt: a life captured and never read back, held by one person or one company, shared with no one. Logbook is the next step on that trail, with the two missing parts.

docs.title: III. Fusing the two sciences
docs.text:
The fusion is not a metaphor; the same structure appears on both sides.

Computer science Human science In Logbook The log is the source of truth; views are derived and disposable Autobiographical memory is reconstructive: we do not replay the past, we rebuild it each time from fragments, and the rebuild drifts (Bartlett, 1932; Loftus) The record is fixed; the recount is a view that can be regenerated, and every sentence links to its evidence so the drift is visible Write-ahead: record before you act on it The experiencing self and the remembering self disagree; memory keeps the peak and the end and drops the duration (Kahneman) Observations are written at the time by instruments; the evening note is the remembering self's line, kept separate and marked as such Idempotent replay; recompute from history when the rules improve Reminiscence: rereading a diary changes what a memory means without changing what happened Engines are versioned and re-run over all history; notes are never touched Hash chain: tamper-evident, verifiable by the holder Narrative identity: a self is the story a person can tell about the connected events of their life (McAdams) A verifiable chain is a story that cannot be quietly rewritten, by you or anyone Access control, capability tokens Trust is built in dyads, one relationship at a time, by reciprocal disclosure (Altman & Taylor's social penetration theory) The circle: a page for a page, named person to named person, no broadcast Garbage collection is forbidden; the log is never pruned Forgetting is the default: the Ebbinghaus curve (1885) drops most of a day within a week Never prune. The instrument remembers so that you may forget freely and reread when it matters Derived metrics: counters, dashboards Gratitude and expressive writing measurably improve wellbeing (Pennebaker, 1986; Emmons & McCullough, 2003) — and extrinsic rewards crowd out intrinsic motivation (Deci) Reveal, never reward: the logbook may show you a first or a milestone; it never scores you

The rule of thumb for any new feature: find its twin on the other side of the table. If a computing idea has no human counterpart, it is plumbing and should be invisible. If a human idea has no computing counterpart, it is a note — and notes are sacred.

docs.title: IV. The statement against the attention economy
docs.text:
Herbert Simon said it in 1971: a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. The industry that followed — Tim Wu called its practitioners the attention merchants — learned to harvest that scarce attention and sell it. Aza Raskin designed infinite scroll in 2006 and has spent years apologising for it. Shoshana Zuboff named the model surveillance capitalism (2019): your record, held by someone else, used to predict and steer you. Neil Postman had warned in 1985 that we were amusing ourselves to death; Jaron Lanier gave ten arguments for deleting your accounts; Cal Newport wrote the manual for leaving.

Every one of these critics described the disease. Fewer built the alternative, and the alternative cannot be "less feed"; it has to be a different object. A feed is other people's present, ranked by a machine to keep you looking, held by a company, measured in your attention. A logbook is your own past, in order, held by you, measured in nothing. The feed asks what is happening? and never lets you finish answering. The logbook asks what happened? and lets you close the book.

The design decisions follow directly:

  • No feed. There is no page that shows other people's lives. There is a page that shows one day of yours.
  • No audience. Sharing is a page handed to a named person who hands one back. There is no post, no follower, no public.
  • No counts. Nothing is liked, viewed, or ranked. Nothing near a person has a number.
  • No engagement loop. One evening question; ignore it forever and nothing happens.
  • No harvest. The files are on your disk. There is no server to sell to, no model trained on you without your key.
  • Reveal, never reward. The logbook can tell you it was your hundredth flight hour or your first time in Portugal. It cannot give you a badge for it.

Social media promised connection and delivered an audience. A logbook makes the old promise honestly: you, your voyage, the few people you choose to show it to — and a book that will still open in fifty years, because it is only paper made of files.

You are the captain of your ship. This is the log.

— bighydro, captain of this one

docs.title: Open problems
docs.text:
A format earns collaborators by stating what it cannot yet do. These are the problems Logbook has not solved, in the order they block v1.0. Each names what is settled, what is not, and where the discussion lives. Corrections to this list are the most welcome pull request there is.

  1. Canonicalisation across languages. RFC 8785 fixes the bytes that are hashed, and two implementations agree on the fixture today. Not settled: whether every JSON library's number formatting survives round trips for the values a life produces (coordinates to seven decimals, nanosecond timestamps from Google Fit, durations as floats). A third implementation in a language with different float semantics (Go, Rust, Swift) would tell us. SPEC §3; conformance/.

  2. Resolving people without a directory. Lines name people by phone, email and handle; resolution lines (RFC 0006) bind them to a person the owner names, with alias hops bounded at three. Not settled: the same person across two records (your Kari and my Kari), merges that later turn out wrong, and a person who asks to be forgotten from someone else's log. There is no global identifier and there must not be one. rfcs/0006; people_merge.

  3. The circle's transport and its trust model. The shared-page bundle (RFC 0025) is signed and verifiable by file. Not settled: how two records find each other, whether a handed page can be revoked, what the recipient may do with it, and how consent is recorded on both sides. The bundle came first so that transport could come second; transport is the first real protocol question. ADR 0009; rfcs/0025.

  4. Sealing without losing verifiability. SPEC v0.3 seals tiers 2 and 3 at rest with age while keeping keyless verify, by chaining over a salted digest with the ciphertext beside it. Not settled: key custody for twenty years, the blinded index's actual leakage under a motivated reader of index.sqlite, and recovery from a lost key for the tiers that matter most. PR #143; docs/rfcs/draft-encryption-at-rest.md.

  5. What a day is. The Day spec (docs/day.md) derives stays, moves, nights and company from location, calendar, photos and transcripts, with named constants. Not settled: a tracker that goes silent indoors, two people with two phones in one car, time zones across a date line, and whether a night aboard a moving vessel is at a place at all. Every constant in policy/stays.json is a hypothesis.

  6. Evidence for company. "Who was there" is confirmed by a timed calendar entry, a transcript or a note, and proposed by a face. Not settled: the error rates of each, how proposals should decay or be dismissed, and how to say "with" about someone who never agreed to be in anyone's log. Rule 5 is the constraint; the mechanism is open.

  7. Schema evolution without rewriting. Profiles are versioned (photo/v1) and lines are never edited. Not settled: how a reader of 2046 handles a payload shape from 2026 it has never seen, and whether a profile may ever be deprecated. The answer so far is "readers tolerate, writers never remove"; it has not been tested across a decade.

  8. Custody. A record that changes hands: a child's until eighteen, an executor's after a death, a vessel's with its sale. Draft RFCs 0029 and 0030 exist. Not settled: almost everything, including whether the law in any jurisdiction recognises a hash chain as a record of custody.

  9. Time. at, end and recorded_at are UTC; tz is the owner's zone at the time; the record's zone localises everything. Not settled: a line whose zone is unknowable (a photo with no location, imported from a service that stripped the offset), leap seconds in a chain that orders by instant, and the IANA database editions two implementations may disagree on.

  10. The second implementation's independence. logbook-ts was written from the spec text alone and agrees on verify, append and show. Not settled: whether it stays independent as its author reads the reference to port the readers, and how to keep two implementations honest when one person maintains both. A third implementer who has read neither is the real test.

If you have solved one of these elsewhere, say so in an issue with the reference. If you think one is wrongly stated, that is the most useful issue of all.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Six passages, each with a gate. Gates are conditions, not dates. A passage begins only when the gate before it is clear.

0 · Harbour — make it true. Encryption at rest merged; one-click install; the readiness gate: three strangers install from the README alone and read back a day of their own life without asking anything.

What has landed, by pull request:

  • The second implementation agrees on every reader SPEC §6.1 names, and CI compares the two on every pull request (#161).
  • The iPhone backup as a source: attach, import-backup, status, verify (#170).
  • Google Takeout product by product, Fit the latest (#202).
  • The days: day and digest (#152), people (#155), year (#157), ledger (#169), tasks (#171), trip (#174), search (#179).
  • The record in a browser from this machine (#153), behind the tier gate as an MCP server (#154), on paper (#188), as a vault (#195), as a static site (#203), on one sheet (#207).
  • The circle by file: a shared day (#168), a shared trip (#194).
  • Sealed at rest: tiers 2 and 3 under age, verify without a key, SPEC v0.3 (#143).
  • The kit: changelog fragments (#180), install in one line per platform (#201), the repository reads in ten minutes (#204).
  • The audit of October 2026 with its three decisions (#210), and its cheap fixes (#205).
  • Of the three decisions, the third has landed: one package, three tiers, shims for 0.6 (#212). Commands and the profile freeze are the rest of this passage.

1 · First strangers — make it theirs. The format meets people who owe its author nothing. Gate: a hundred strangers with a Day page; three adapters merged from people we have never met; the first bug report about their data, not ours.

2 · The circle — make it shared. Pages handed between records by file. Gate: ten households with two or more records exchanging pages; an agent other than the reference's reads a logbook through the gate.

3 · v1.0 — make it final. Eighteen profiles frozen; both implementations agree on every reader; the specification tagged 1.0 with the conformance badge.

4 · Everyone — make it easy. From the terminal to the kitchen table: a hosted viewer you can leave, the record on a phone, the TypeScript implementation as a web application. Gate: ten thousand records; a product nobody involved built says "reads a logbook".

5 · The standard — make it last. Certification, custody in use, a foundation holding the specification. Gate: the format is used by people who have never heard of its author and would not notice if the author stopped.

What is deliberately not on this list: a feed, an account, a server, a company.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This software stores a person's whole life. Treat every bug as if it were serious.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Report a vulnerability privately: through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting on this repository, or to the address in the repository profile. Never in a public issue. You will get a reply within 48 hours. The fix ships before the report is disclosed, and the advisory names you unless you ask it not to.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
What is protected. One folder on a machine the owner controls: the record (logbook/<YYYY>/<MM>.jsonl), the notes, the attachments, the policy files, the owner's signing key and the sealing identity. The record is the whole of a person's whereabouts, company, words, health and money, so a copy of the folder is the asset, and the chain head is the proof that nobody changed it.

Who the adversary is. Anyone who obtains the files: a stolen laptop, a backup disk in the wrong hands, a cloud drive the folder was mistakenly placed in, malware on the machine, a member of the owner's circle who was handed one page and wants the rest, and an agent that was given read access and asked for more. The adversary is not assumed to hold the owner's key.

What is defended today.

  • Integrity. Every line carries the hash of the one before (SPEC §3). verify finds any edit, removal or reordering, and a broken chain is an error, never repaired silently. Nothing in the code updates or deletes a line; a correction is a new line that retracts an old one.
  • Confidentiality at rest. Tier 1 is plain. Tiers 2 and 3, the words, the names, the amounts and the samples, are sealed with age to recipients the owner holds (SPEC §2 and §4, RFC 0029, ADR 0020) once the record names them: the identity never enters the record and is never in a variable on disk, and there are two recipients at least, so a lost laptop loses nothing and a lost key loses the words of tiers 2 and 3 and never the chain. The envelope stays plain, so an adversary with the files learns the shape of the owner's days, a message from which source at what time, and none of the words; RFC 0029 §2 states that limit. The chain is verifiable without any key; with the key, verify opens every sealed line and checks it against its digest. Attachments a sealed line points at are sealed under the same name, and the index, a plaintext locator, lives in the user's cache directory with chat ids blinded, never in the record.
  • Nothing leaves. There is no server and no account, and reading never opens a connection. Every reader touches the record and the tables shipped in the package, nothing else. tests/test_no_network.py replaces the socket, urllib, http.client and, where installed, the httpx, requests and websockets request paths with ones that record and refuse every connection, runs every reader against the demo record and every page of serve through it, and fails if any of them asked for one, whatever it printed or caught. A socket opens only behind a command that says so: sync for the live source it names, transcribe --fetch-model and its siblings for a model this machine has not got, serve listening on 127.0.0.1 and refusing any other host. A change that needs a reader to fetch anything is wrong; a new reader goes into that test's list.
  • The circle. A shared page or trip is a bundle signed with the owner's Ed25519 key, holding only the lines the owner's policy/crossing.json lets cross to that one named person at their tier ceiling. The receiver verifies the signature and keeps the bundle beside the record, never in its chain. The default ceiling for every destination, including an agent over MCP, is tier 1: the shape of the days and no note, message, name, health or money.
  • Adapters. An adapter is untrusted code that runs without network by default, never writes to its source, and can only append. An app store is opened read-only after its schema is confirmed with PRAGMA table_info; a phone backup is copied into inbox/ and never modified.
  • Agents. An agent over MCP may read within its ceiling and run adapters; it cannot write a note, a confirmation or a visibility decision. Tier 3 reaches it only when the policy file allows it and the server was started with --allow-tier-3.

What is not defended yet, and what to do about it.

  • Older copies. Sealing protects the copies made after it is turned on; a backup or sync taken before seal --all holds the plaintext, and the command says so once. A record without recipients is plain text at every tier. In both cases the protection is the one the operating system gives: full-disk encryption on every machine and backup disk that holds the folder, and never a folder a sync client owns (logbook setup refuses one).
  • The shape of the days. The envelope of a sealed line is plain by design, so the sources, kinds and times of tiers 2 and 3 are readable with the files; a sealed line in a shared page is ciphertext the receiver cannot open until the page reseals it (RFC 0029 §15), and search does not search sealed lines.
  • The keys. The sharing key is a file under ~/.config/logbook/share/, the sealing identity one under ~/.config/logbook/identities/, both outside the record and readable by the owner alone, so a copy of the folder cannot sign as the owner or open the sealed lines. Whoever holds those files can; neither is protected by a passphrase, because a prompt breaks unattended reads, so the disk they sit on is encrypted. A lost sharing key means a new one, and every member of the circle learns the new public half; a lost sealing identity is covered by the recovery identity key init --recovery printed once for paper, and key remove-recipient reseals the record without the lost one.
  • Malware with the owner's privileges can read the files and append to the chain. The chain shows that something was appended and when; it cannot show who typed it.
  • What a page reveals. A member who receives a page at tier 2 receives the notes on it. The policy file is the owner's decision; an export's --dry-run lists what would cross, and an agent's answer says how many lines sat above its ceiling and were left out, so the owner can see what a raise would release.

Out of scope. The security of the services the exports come from, the phone's own backup encryption (which import-backup decrypts only with the owner's password, locally), and the model files transcribe, promises --judge and describe download on request.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text: Dependencies are pinned in uv.lock and raised by Dependabot. Every release wheel carries SLSA provenance and is published to PyPI through trusted publishing; nothing is signed by a human's laptop. gitleaks and the PII check run on every commit, so no secret and no real identifier enters the tree.

docs.title: Logbook format — specification v0.3
docs.text:
Status: draft. License: CC0. Anyone may implement this without asking.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

docs.title: 1. The folder
docs.text:
<root>/
  logbook.json            identity and chain head
  logbook/<YYYY>/<MM>.jsonl   the record
  notes/<YYYY>/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md   free text, optional
  attachments/<sha256>    optional; content-addressed files a line points at (§1.1)
  inbox/                  optional; not part of conformance

A derived locator (index.sqlite, ADR 0007) is disposable and not part of conformance; the reference keeps it in the user's cache directory, outside this folder, so a copy of the folder carries no locator (RFC 0029 §8). An implementation MAY keep one inside the folder.

logbook.json:

{"format": "logbook/0.3", "owner_id": "<uuid>", "created_at": "<RFC3339 UTC>",
 "timezone": "<IANA tz>", "seq": 4181, "head": "<hex sha256>",
 "recipients": ["age1x5ut7lplvtgkzcnvtjux674z32mu5q72r6ffaxemxtg9g08p7g5qa8ytxl", "age1…"],
 "lineage": [{"from_format": "logbook/0.2", "from_head": "<hex sha256>", "migrated_at": "<RFC3339 UTC>"}]}

recipients lists the age X25519 recipients (the public halves) that tiers 2–3 are sealed to (§4). It is present in a record that seals, with two entries at least; a record without it, or with an empty list, seals nothing. The private identity is never in this folder (RFC 0029 §6).

seq and head are those of the last line in chain order (§3). A record with no lines has seq 0 and head GENESIS. GENESIS is the string of 64 ASCII 0 characters, 0000…0000; it is a named constant, not the digest of anything, and it is also the prev of the first line (§3).

lineage is present only in a record that was migrated from an earlier format, or that sealed its past (§3.1).

Writers MUST preserve keys of logbook.json they do not know: read the file, change seq and head, write everything else back. An implementation that rewrites the file from a fixed set of keys drops lineage, and whatever a later version adds, the first time it appends.

docs.title: 1.1 Attachments
docs.text:
Some observations refer to a file too large, binary or private to put in a line: a transcript, a photo, a voice message. A line MUST NOT inline such content. The file is stored once, named by its own SHA-256, and the line points at it.

A file lives at <root>/attachments/<sha256>, where <sha256> is the lowercase hex digest of the file's exact bytes: no extension, no subdirectories.

A payload references it as an object of this shape:

{"sha256": "<hex sha256>", "path": "attachments/<hex sha256>", "bytes": 48213, "media_type": "text/markdown"}

path is relative to the record root. bytes is the length of the file. media_type is an IANA media type. A profile MAY name the field as it likes (content, media, attachments) but MUST use this shape.

The store is write-once: a digest is written once and never rewritten. Two lines that point at the same bytes share one file; this is how re-importing a source de-duplicates. Attachments are record, not cache (ADR 0001): they are never pruned.

The chain covers lines, not bytes. The digest is inside the line, so tampering with the file is detectable, but the file is not in the hash chain. verify MUST NOT fail because an attachment is missing; it MUST report missing attachments separately and exit 0 when the chain is intact. A verifier MAY check the digests of present files; a file whose bytes do not match its name is an error.

Sealed files.
